assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Glycoprotein
items.clue: A membrane protein with a carbohydrate chain covalently attached.

items.label: Selective permeability
items.clue: The property of a membrane that allows some substances to cross while others cannot.

items.label: Glycolipid
items.clue: A membrane lipid with a carbohydrate chain covalently attached to its hydrophilic head.

items.label: Amphipathic
items.clue: Describes a molecule that has both a hydrophilic (water-attracting) region and a hydrophobic (water-repelling) region.

questions.stem: Why do phospholipids form a bilayer when they are mixed with water?

options.text: Hydrophilic heads face the water and hydrophobic tails are shielded from it, so the sheet forms spontaneously.
Enzymes in the cell join the phospholipids together into a sheet, using energy released from ATP.
The whole molecule repels water, so the phospholipids gather away from it as a droplet of oil.
Covalent bonds form between neighbouring phospholipids, linking them into one rigid sheet of molecules.

questions.stem: Which of these particles crosses a pure phospholipid bilayer, with no proteins present, least readily?

options.text: A carbon dioxide molecule, which is larger than a water molecule
An oxygen molecule, which needs a protein to cross the bilayer
A sodium ion, which is small but charged and hydrophilic
A water molecule, which is very small and also polar

questions.explanation: The hydrophobic core has very low permeability to hydrophilic particles, including ions and polar molecules. A charged sodium ion cannot enter the hydrocarbon core, so it has the lowest permeability of the four.

questions.stem: A cell is respiring rapidly, so its internal oxygen concentration is low. How do oxygen molecules enter the cell?

options.text: They diffuse through a channel protein that is specific for oxygen and opens when needed
They are moved in by a pump protein using ATP, because the cell needs oxygen urgently
They move in and out randomly until the concentrations are equal, then stop moving
They pass between the phospholipids by simple diffusion down their gradient

questions.stem: Which statement about membrane proteins is correct?

options.text: Integral proteins are embedded in one or both lipid layers, while peripheral proteins are attached to a surface.
Integral proteins all span the whole bilayer, while peripheral proteins are embedded in only one layer.
Integral and peripheral proteins are both transport proteins, differing only in the substance they carry.
Glycoproteins carry their carbohydrate on both faces of the membrane, so the two surfaces are identical.

questions.stem: Some cells lining the kidney tubules have large numbers of aquaporins in their plasma membranes. What is the effect of these aquaporins?

options.text: They pump water across the membrane against its gradient, using ATP energy.
They allow water to cross the membrane, which is otherwise impossible for the bilayer.
They greatly increase the rate at which water can cross the membrane by osmosis.
They let water move in the direction the cell needs, whatever the solute concentrations.

questions.stem: A potassium channel in a cell membrane is open. Which statement describes the movement of ions through it?

options.text: Potassium ions and any other ions of similar size diffuse through the open pore.
Potassium ions are moved through in whichever direction the cell requires.
Potassium ions are carried through using energy from the hydrolysis of ATP.
Potassium ions diffuse through, down their gradient, with no ATP used.

questions.explanation: A channel provides a hydrophilic route through the hydrophobic core for one specific ion. The ions move by facilitated diffusion, down their concentration gradient, and no energy from ATP is needed.

questions.stem: Which statement about glycoproteins in the plasma membrane is correct?

options.text: Their carbohydrate is on the cytoplasmic side and is respired when the cell lacks glucose.
Their carbohydrate projects from both faces of the membrane so that either face can be recognised.
Their carbohydrate is on the extracellular side and is used in cell recognition and adhesion.
They are transport proteins whose carbohydrate forms the channel through which sugars enter the cell.

questions.stem: A lipid is found to form a continuous sheet-like bilayer when shaken with water. Which property must the lipid have?

options.text: It must be entirely hydrophobic, so that all of its molecules cluster together away from water.
It must be amphipathic, with a hydrophilic region and a hydrophobic region in each molecule.
It must be able to form covalent bonds with neighbouring lipid molecules in the sheet.
It must be acted on by an enzyme that assembles the molecules into the bilayer.

questions.stem: Why does a lipid bilayer that contains a high proportion of unsaturated fatty acids remain fluid at low temperatures?

options.text: The double bonds hold neighbouring tails rigidly together, giving the bilayer a fixed structure.
The kinked tails cannot pack closely, so the lipids have a lower melting point.
The bilayer's fluidity does not depend on temperature, so its fatty acids make no difference.
The unsaturated tails are straighter than saturated tails, so they slide past one another easily.

questions.stem: Which statement describes cholesterol in an animal cell membrane?

options.text: It lies within the bilayer between phospholipids and acts solely to reduce membrane fluidity.
It is attached to the outer surface of the bilayer and makes the membrane stiffer and stronger.
It is attached to the outer surface of the bilayer and carries carbohydrate used in cell recognition.
It lies in the bilayer between phospholipids and adjusts fluidity in both directions.

questions.stem: Acetylcholine released at a synapse binds to nicotinic acetylcholine receptors on the postsynaptic membrane. What happens as a result?

options.text: The receptor opens and the acetylcholine molecules pass through it into the postsynaptic neuron.
The receptor uses ATP to pump sodium ions into the postsynaptic neuron, depolarizing it.
The receptor stays closed until the membrane potential changes, then it opens.
The receptor's channel opens and sodium ions diffuse into the neuron down their gradient.

questions.stem: Which sequence correctly describes one cycle of the sodium–potassium pump?

options.text: Three potassium ions bind inside; ATP phosphorylates the pump; they are released outside; two sodium ions then bind and are released inside.
Three sodium ions bind inside; ATP phosphorylates the pump; they are released outside; two potassium ions bind and are released inside.
One sodium ion binds inside; ATP phosphorylates the pump; it is released outside; one potassium ion binds and is released inside.
Three sodium ions bind inside; the pump opens when the membrane potential changes; they diffuse out; two potassium ions diffuse in.

questions.stem: How do cells lining the nephron reabsorb glucose from the filtrate when the glucose concentration inside the cells is already higher than in the filtrate?

options.text: Glucose diffuses in through the lipid bilayer down its own concentration gradient
A cotransporter hydrolyses ATP directly to move glucose in against its gradient
Sodium–potassium pumps carry glucose into the cell together with the potassium
A cotransporter moves glucose in with sodium ions moving down their gradient

questions.stem: How do adjacent cells adhere to one another to form a tissue?

options.text: Cell-adhesion molecules in each cell's membrane bind to those on the neighbouring cell, with different CAMs used for different junctions.
The fluid plasma membranes of the two cells fuse where they touch, so the two cells share one continuous membrane.
A single universal cell-adhesion molecule links every cell to its neighbours in every type of tissue in the body.
The carbohydrate chains of glycoproteins on one cell are covalently bonded to the lipid bilayer of the adjacent cell.
